evals.prompt: Review only measurable performance regressions. Accepted workload: ListInvoices serves 1,000-item pages at 200 requests/second under a p95 150 ms budget; baseline uses one batched query, at most 8 bounded dependency calls, and 2 allocations per encoded item. The change performs one customer query and one JSON marshal per item inside the loop, launches one goroutine per invoice, appends retained 1 MiB buffers to a cache, and claims improvement from a single 50 ms microbenchmark run without -benchmem, repetitions, environment control, benchstat, profiles, or end-to-end evidence.
evals.expected_output: Report I/O and fan-out amplification, allocation/retention and contention/tail risk, plus benchmark evidence defects against the accepted workload and budget.
expectations: Names the per-item query/marshal scaling and unbounded goroutine fan-out as workload amplification.
Identifies allocation or retained-memory risk from the large cached buffers.
Rejects the one-run microbenchmark as proof because workload, allocation, repetition, control, practical significance, or end-to-end fit is missing.
Requests the narrow benchmark, benchstat, profile, trace, query-count, or load evidence that matches each material claim.

evals.prompt: Review only accepted performance behavior. The changed hot path names its production-representative workload, scale dimension, p95 budget, baseline, environment, and metric. It reduces round trips and copies without changing results; active work, queues, fan-out, retries, blocking I/O, and retention remain bounded and cancellation-aware. Repeated -benchmem runs and benchstat show a practically meaningful gain under stable fixtures, while matching CPU and allocation profiles explain it. The simpler ownership shape remains. No performance policy is missing or changed.
evals.expected_output: Return no performance findings without padding, invented budgets, micro-optimization advice, or neighboring-domain warnings.
expectations: Returns no performance findings.
Does not invent workloads, budgets, benchmarks, profiles, or optimization complexity.
Does not pad the result with concurrency, DB/cache, reliability, or architecture findings.

evals.prompt: Accepted performance budgets and fresh benchmarks show no latency, throughput, allocation, contention, I/O, or scaling regression. The changed worker protocol calls wg.Add after launching a goroutine, closes the same channel from both producer and receiver, and can wait forever after cancellation. Review owner arbitration only.
evals.expected_output: Name go-concurrency as the single primary owner for WaitGroup ordering, channel-close ownership, cancellation unblock, and join defects; emit no duplicate performance finding.
expectations: Names exactly go-concurrency as the primary review owner.
Identifies concrete happens-before, channel ownership, cancellation, or join mechanics as the decisive axis.
Emits no performance finding because measured performance conformance is stated as preserved.

evals.prompt: A serialization path is changed and a small microbenchmark becomes faster, but no accepted workload, traffic or data scale, latency/throughput/allocation budget, baseline environment, representative benchmark boundary, or required profile/load evidence exists. Correctness is unchanged and no unbounded amplification is visible from the diff. Review without choosing performance policy.
evals.expected_output: Hand off the missing workload, budget, and proof contract to go-performance without inventing targets or reporting an unsupported regression.
expectations: Names go-performance as the unresolved decision owner.
Does not invent scale, latency, throughput, allocation, environment, benchmark, profile, or load targets.
Does not report a performance regression when neither accepted policy nor concrete amplification supports one.

evals.prompt: Use go-performance for the account-summary endpoint. Production evidence shows 60% small tenants with 20 rows, 35% typical tenants with 500 rows, 5% large tenants with 20,000 rows, and one hot tenant producing 30% of peak requests. Peak is 800 requests per second with a 3x 20-second burst; warm, cold, and cache-down modes all occur. Current representative load results are p50 35 ms, p95 190 ms, p99 780 ms, 18 MiB/s allocations, 3.2 CPU cores, and DB pool wait p95 45 ms. Product requires p95 at most 150 ms and p99 at most 400 ms for small and typical tenants at peak, while large tenants may move to an already accepted paginated representation. Capacity is four replicas at 1 CPU and 512 MiB each. Write the performance contract with workload buckets, critical path and bottleneck hypothesis, latency/throughput/allocation/GC/memory/contention budgets, option choice, reproducible benchmark/load/profile/trace evidence, regression thresholds, telemetry, canary, and rollback. Do not choose a cache consistency model or service topology.
evals.expected_output: A measurable performance specification tied to representative workload buckets, explicit budgets and bottleneck evidence, claim-matched proof with variance and regression thresholds, and runtime rollout actions without inventing neighboring mechanisms.
expectations: Keeps small, typical, large, hot-tenant, warm, cold, cache-down, peak, and burst workload dimensions explicit instead of reporting only an aggregate.
Maps the critical path and uses the provided latency, allocation, CPU, and DB-wait baseline to state a falsifiable bottleneck hypothesis.
Defines relevant latency, throughput, allocation, GC, memory, contention, pool, and capacity budgets without inventing unsupported targets.
Chooses or compares the least-complex plausible option before pooling, caching, PGO, or fan-out and records forced API or DB/cache consequences only.

Distinguishes microbenchmark, scenario benchmark, representative load, profile, and trace evidence and includes controlled fixtures, sample count, variance, pass/fail, and per-bucket regression thresholds.
Names bounded runtime metrics, aggregation windows, canary checkpoints, owners, rollback triggers, and actions proportional to the performance claim.
Does not choose cache consistency, DB/cache mechanism, system topology, or package placement.

evals.prompt: The accepted performance contract already fixes critical paths, production-derived workload buckets and skew, warm/cold/degraded modes, latency and throughput budgets, allocation/GC/memory/contention/capacity limits, baseline evidence, option choice, reproducible benchmark/load/profile/trace protocols, sample and variance rules, per-bucket regression thresholds, bounded telemetry, canary checkpoints, and rollback actions. A follow-up only renames an internal helper with identical generated code and measurements. Apply go-performance.
evals.expected_output: No new performance decision, with the accepted workload, budget, evidence, and rollout contract unchanged.
expectations: Returns no_new_decision_required or explicit unchanged performance constraints.
Does not invent new budgets, optimizations, benchmarks, profiles, traces, telemetry, or rollout gates.
Leaves helper naming and placement to implementation ownership without padding.

evals.prompt: The accepted performance contract fixes the account-summary workload buckets, p95 and p99 targets, throughput, allocation and memory ceilings, cache-warm and cache-down measurements, benchmark and load protocols, regression threshold, canary telemetry, and rollback trigger. The remaining decisions are whether Postgres or Redis is authoritative, acceptable staleness, cache key dimensions, TTL and invalidation, stampede control, and cache-down fallback semantics. Apply go-performance only.
evals.expected_output: Only the forced performance budgets and proof constraints, with go-db-cache owning authority, freshness, keying, invalidation, stampede, and fallback decisions.
expectations: Names go-db-cache as owner of source of truth, freshness, key dimensions, TTL, invalidation, stampede, and cache-down behavior.
Carries only the accepted latency, throughput, resource, workload, and cache-state proof constraints.
Does not select Postgres or Redis authority, a TTL, invalidation mechanism, cache topology, or fallback semantics.

evals.prompt: Make report generation ten times faster and write the final performance contract now. No operation class, critical path, input sizes, traffic mix, concurrency, tenant skew, dependency or cache state, current baseline, production evidence, user-visible latency objective, throughput target, resource envelope, regression tolerance, or rollout authority is available. Choose numeric budgets, benchmark fixtures, optimization, and pass/fail threshold so coding can start.
evals.expected_output: A blocked performance specification that refuses to invent workload, baseline, target authority, optimization, or proof thresholds.
expectations: Stops on the unknown critical path, representative workload, baseline, target authority, resource envelope, regression tolerance, and rollout policy.
Requests or names the product/service/capacity owners and production evidence needed to set the contract.
Does not invent a ten-times target interpretation, numeric budgets, fixtures, optimization mechanism, or pass/fail threshold.
